## 6. Embedded Systems, Silicon Real-Time, Thermal, and Hardware Safety

Response-time analysis keeps the Liu–Layland letters of its literature, but only inside that model and only with a task index $i$, $j$, or $k$: $C_i$ (worst-case execution time), $B_i$ (blocking), $I_i$ (interference), $J_i$ (release jitter), $T_i$ (period), $R_i$ (worst-case response time), and $D_i$ (relative deadline, which is $\Deadline$ of task $i$ in the series' terms), as in $R_i = C_i + B_i + I_i \le D_i$. Outside that model these letters keep their table meanings.

::: {tbl-colwidths="[14,22,12,52]"}

| **Symbol**                     | **Definition**                | **Unit**      | **Notes**                                                                                                                                                             |
|:-------------------------------|:------------------------------|:--------------|:----------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------|
| **$\DcBusBulkCapacitance$**    | **DC Bus Bulk Capacitance**   | $\mu\text{F}$ | Inverter decoupling capacitor bank buffering transient inductive voltage collapse.                                                                                    |
| **$\TelemetryFreshnessBound$** | **Telemetry Freshness Bound** | $\text{ms}$   | Maximum allowable age of sensor telemetry before an interlock trips: $\TelemetryFreshnessBound \le \InitialAndCeilingError / \SpeedBound$.                            |
| **$\ClockOffset$**             | **Clock Offset**              | $\mu\text{s}$ | Offset of one clock from another, estimated from a timestamp exchange as $\ClockOffset = [(t_2 - t_1) - (t_4 - t_3)]/2$; its one-way path delay is $T_{\text{prop}}$. |
| **$\TimingJitter$**            | **Timing Jitter**             | $\mu\text{s}$ | Standard deviation of a nominally periodic event's timing about its schedule.                                                                                         |
| **$\SynchronizationBlackout$** | **Synchronization Blackout**  | $\text{s}$    | Interval during which a node receives no synchronization message and free-runs on its own clock.                                                                      |

:::

## The Energy Corollary {#sec-notation-conventions-energy-corollary-a1da .unlisted}

With effective per-byte and per-operation costs, workload energy is approximated as:
$$\TotalEnergy \approx \DataVolume \times \EnergyPerByteMoved + O \times \EnergyPerOperationCompute$$

::: {tbl-colwidths="[10,25,15,50]"}

| **Symbol**                       | **Definition**            | **Unit**    | **Notes**                                                                                  |
|:---------------------------------|:--------------------------|:------------|:-------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------|
| **$\EnergyPerByteMoved$**        | **Energy per Byte Moved** | joules/byte | Effective movement cost; total energy also depends on bytes moved and operations executed. |
| **$\EnergyPerOperationCompute$** | **Energy per Operation**  | joules/FLOP | Energy cost of a single arithmetic operation.                                              |
| **$\TotalEnergy$**               | **Total Energy**          | joules      | Total energy consumed by an ML workload, decomposed into data-movement and compute terms.  |

:::

## Deep Learning Notation {#sec-notation-conventions-deep-learning-notation-b40d .unlisted}

This book follows standard deep learning conventions [@goodfellow2016deep] with explicit disambiguation for systems variables.

::: {tbl-colwidths="[8,20,72]"}

| **Symbol**                    | **Definition**               | **Unit**     | **Notes**                                                                                      |
|:------------------------------|:-----------------------------|:-------------|:-----------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------|
| **$\AttentionHeadDimension$** | **Attention Head Dimension** | Integer      | Per-head hidden dimension in attention layers.                                                 |
| **$\HiddenDimension$**        | **Hidden Dimension**         | Integer      | Hidden feature dimension $d$ of a neural layer or representation.                              |
| **$\HiddenDimensionFour$**    | **Hidden / Time Dimension**  | Integer      | Alternate dimension or time index $p$.                                                         |
| **$\LayerIndex$**             | **Layer Index**              | Integer      | Index $\ell$ for a neural network layer.                                                       |
| **$\LossFunction$**           | **Loss Function**            | Scalar       | The objective function minimized during training.                                              |
| **$\ModelParameters$**        | **Model Parameters**         | Vector       | Trainable model parameter vector or weights $\theta$.                                          |
| **$\NumberOfLayers$**         | **Number of Layers**         | Integer      | Total number of layers in a network.                                                           |
| **$\SequenceLength$**         | **Sequence Length**          | Integer      | Input context or sequence length $S$ in tokens.                                                |
| **$\TrainingDistribution$**   | **Training Distribution**    | Distribution | The data distribution at training time.                                                        |
| **$\WeightMemory$**           | **Weight Memory**            | bytes        | Memory occupied by model weights ($P \times \text{bytes-per-parameter}$); the core's quantity. |

:::

Latin matrices and vectors are set in bold ($\mathbf{W}$, $\mathbf{x}$); scalars, dimensions, indices, and individual matrix entries stay italic ($N$, $d$, $i$, $W_{ij}$). The generic parameter symbol $\theta$ is the one conventional exception and stays italic. Local matrix algebra follows the same bold rule: matrix operands are bold ($\mathbf{A}$, $\mathbf{B}$, $\mathbf{C}$), as in general matrix multiply (GEMM) $\mathbf{C}=\alpha \mathbf{A}\mathbf{B}+\beta \mathbf{C}$. The bold form marks a matrix operand and is distinct from the italic scalar batch size $B$, which remains batch size in scalar contexts. A GEMM's scalar dimensions are $M$, $N$, and $K$ ($\mathbf{A}$ is $M \times K$, $\mathbf{B}$ is $K \times N$). Asymptotic cost is written $\mathcal{O}(\cdot)$, which keeps it distinct from the operation count $O$.

## Performance, Serving, and Memory Notation {#sec-notation-conventions-performance-serving-memory .unlisted}

Reusable performance and serving quantities follow the same collision-avoidance rule as the iron law. Rates use $R$ or descriptive Greek symbols; request counts use $\RequestConcurrency$ rather than overloading $N$; queue utilization uses a subscripted $\rho$ so bare $\rho$ remains available for other ratio models.

```{=latex}

\renewcommand{\arraystretch}{1.3}
```

The Roofline Model uses $I$ as the independent variable.                                                                                                                                 |

The subscript keeps bare $\lambda$ free for fitted sensitivities.                                                                                                                                 |

| **$\LinkBandwidth$**                  | **Link Bandwidth**                     | bytes/s       | Inter-device network link bandwidth $\beta$.                                                                                                                                                                            |

## Units and Precision {#sec-notation-conventions-units-precision-fdaf .unlisted}

*   Physical units: This book uses SI (metric) units throughout, including meters, kilograms, seconds, watts, and °C, consistent with standard engineering and scientific practice. Where source data was originally reported in imperial units, the book converts to SI and notes the original values parenthetically. A space always separates the number from the unit (for example, 100 ms, 2 TB/s).
*   Data and memory: This book uses **decimal SI prefixes only**: KB = $10^3$ bytes, MB = $10^6$, GB = $10^9$, TB = $10^{12}$. Binary-prefixed units do not appear in prose; model sizes, activation footprints, throughputs, and transfer volumes are reported in decimal units (for example, 2 TB/s, 102 MB). Hardware memory capacities are the one exception: they keep the vendor's nameplate figure and label, so an accelerator sold as 80 GB holds $80 \times 2^{30}$ bytes.
*   Compute: The notation distinguishes operation counts from rates. Total work uses FLOPs (for example, GFLOPs, TFLOPs), while throughput uses FLOP/s with decimal prefixes (for example, GFLOP/s, TFLOP/s).
    *   1 TFLOP = $10^{12}$ FLOPs
    *   1 TFLOP/s = $10^{12}$ FLOPs per second
    *   Arithmetic intensity conventionally uses FLOP/byte as a unit ratio (floating-point operations per byte moved). This is a ratio unit, not a total-work symbol or throughput symbol.
*   Power: Power carries a subscript ($P_{\text{avg}}$, $P_{\text{device}}$, $P_{\text{cluster}}$); bare $P$ remains parameter count.
*   Latency percentiles: Written p50, p95, and p99 in upright type, inside math as well as in prose.
*   Currency: Dollar amounts use the dollar sign (`$`); unless otherwise noted, dollar-denominated costs are U.S. dollars (USD).
*   Precision:
    *   **FP64**: Double precision (8 bytes)
    *   **FP32**: Single precision (4 bytes)
    *   **TF32**: TensorFloat-32 (19-bit Tensor Core compute mode; inputs and storage remain FP32)
    *   **FP16**: Half precision (2 bytes, standard range)
    *   **BF16**: Brain float (2 bytes, wide dynamic range)
    *   **FP8**: Quarter precision (1 byte, E4M3 or E5M2 format)
    *   **FP4**: 4-bit floating-point format
    *   **INT8**: 8-bit integer (1 byte)
    *   **INT4**: 4-bit integer; lower integer precisions follow the same uppercase `INTn` pattern (for example, INT3, INT2)

## Quick Reference: Resolving Collisions {#sec-notation-conventions-quick-reference-resolving-collisions-a9cf .unlisted}

Common collision points in ML Systems literature include:

::: {tbl-colwidths="[15,20,25,40]"}

| **Symbol**         | **Definition**   | **Unit**    | **Notes**                                             |
|:-------------------|:-----------------|:------------|:------------------------------------------------------|
| **$\BatchSize$**   | **Batch Size**   | Bandwidth   | **Batch Size**. Use $\Bandwidth$ for bandwidth.       |
| **$\DatasetSize$** | **Dataset Size** | Data Volume | **Dataset Size**. Use $\DataVolume$ for bytes moved.  |
| **$\Loss$**        | **Loss**         | Latency     | **Loss** $(\mathcal{L})$. Use $\Latency$ for latency. |
| **$\Parameters$**  | **Parameters**   | Peak FLOP/s | **Parameters**. Use $\PeakRate$ for peak rate.        |

:::

As a general principle, ML conventions take precedence for single letters, while systems concepts get subscripts or multi-letter symbols. This reflects the primary audience (ML practitioners learning systems) and preserves compatibility with the vast ML literature.

```{=latex}
\part{key:mainmatter}
```
